steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a detailed comparison of RNA (ribonucleic acid) and DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid):

1. Basic Function  
   • DNA  
     – Long‐term storage of genetic information  
     – Blueprint for all proteins and functional RNAs in the cell  
   • RNA  
     – Multiple roles in gene expression and regulation  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA) conveys instructions from DNA to ribosomes  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) help assemble proteins  
     – Other noncoding RNAs (e.g., microRNA) regulate gene activity  

2. Sugar Component  
   • DNA  
     – Contains deoxyribose sugar (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon)  
   • RNA  
     – Contains ribose sugar (has an –OH group on the 2′ carbon)  

3. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • DNA  
     – Adenine (A), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G), Thymine (T)  
   • RNA  
     – Adenine (A), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G), Uracil (U) (replaces thymine)  

4. Strand Structure  
   • DNA  
     – Typically double‐stranded helix (antiparallel strands held by hydrogen bonds)  
     – Very stable under a range of conditions  
   • RNA  
     – Usually single‐stranded, but can fold back on itself to form hairpins, loops, bulges  
     – Less chemically stable (more prone to hydrolysis)  

5. Cellular Location  
   • DNA  
     – In eukaryotes: housed in the nucleus (also in mitochondria, chloroplasts)  
     – In prokaryotes: in the cytoplasm (nucleoid region)  
   • RNA  
     – Transcribed in the nucleus (eukaryotes), then travels to cytoplasm  
     – Found throughout the cell, including ribosomes, cytosol, and organelles  

6. Synthesis and Turnover  
   • DNA  
     – Replicated once per cell cycle by DNA polymerases  
     – Very low turnover; long half‐life in the cell  
   • RNA  
     – Synthesized (transcribed) by RNA polymerases as needed  
     – Relatively short half‐lives; constantly made and degraded  

7. Error Checking and Repair  
   • DNA  
     – Extensive proofreading and repair mechanisms (mismatch repair, excision repair)  
   • RNA  
     – Little to no proofreading; errors in transcription are tolerated because RNAs are transient  

8. Size and Complexity  
   • DNA  
     – Genomes range from thousands (viruses) to billions (plants, animals) of base pairs  
   • RNA  
     – Individual transcripts vary from ~20 nucleotides (microRNA) to tens of thousands (long noncoding RNAs)  

9. Chemical Stability and Practical Implications  
   • DNA  
     – More stable—suited for long‐term storage, archival DNA sequencing  
   • RNA  
     – Less stable—must be handled carefully in labs (RNases everywhere)  
     – Its instability is also an advantage: gene expression can be turned on/off rapidly  

In summary, DNA is the durable archive of genetic instructions, built from deoxyribose, using thymine, and organized as a double helix. RNA is the versatile, more reactive copy/working molecule, built from ribose, using uracil, usually single‐stranded, and key to translating those instructions into proteins and regulating gene activity.
